How many tuples are in this relational-algebra expression, and how many rows does `SELECT cid FROM enrolled` return?

```formula
π cid (Enrolled)
where

cid: the course-code attribute
Enrolled: the enrolment relation above
In words: the course codes in Enrolled, as a relation.
```

options.explanation: SQL does not remove duplicates unless you ask with `DISTINCT`; this assumes SQL uses set semantics.
This forgets that projection in relational algebra produces a set, so duplicate DB and OS values collapse.
Correct. Projection yields the set {DB, OS, LA}. SQL works on bags, so it returns one row per enrolment: 6 rows.
Reversed: the algebra removes duplicates, SQL keeps them.

workedExample:
1. Project Enrolled on cid: DB, OS, LA, DB, DB, OS.
2. Algebra: a relation is a set, so each value is kept once:

```formula
π cid (Enrolled) = {DB, OS, LA}
where
π: projection: keep only the listed attributes, then remove duplicate tuples
cid: the course-code attribute
Enrolled: the enrolment relation, 6 tuples
{ }: a set: distinct values, no order
DB, OS, LA: the three course codes
In words: six enrolments mention only three different courses, so the projection has 3 tuples.
```

prompt: Relational algebra can be built from a minimal set of six operators, with the rest defined in terms of them. Which of these belong to that minimal set? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Product is primitive; every join is defined as a product followed by a selection.
Correct. Difference is primitive, and intersection is derived from it: the intersection of R and S is R minus the part of R that is not in S.
Derived: it is a product, a selection on equal shared attributes, and a projection to drop the duplicate columns.
Derived from difference: R minus (R minus S). A common mistake is to assume all three set operators are primitive.
Correct. Rename is needed so that, for example, a relation can be combined with a copy of itself.

workedExample:
The six primitives are selection σ, projection π, rename ρ, union ∪, difference − and Cartesian product ×. Everything else is shorthand:

```formula
R ⋈θ S = σθ (R × S)
R ∩ S = R − (R − S)
where
R, S: any two relations
⋈θ: theta join: combine tuples satisfying the condition θ (theta)
⋈: natural join (no condition): match on all shared attribute names
σθ: selection σ (the Greek letter sigma) with condition θ: keep tuples where θ is true
π: projection (pi): keep only the listed attributes
ρ: rename (rho): give a relation or attribute a new name
×: Cartesian product: every tuple of R paired with every tuple of S
∪: union: tuples in either input
∩: intersection: tuples in both
−: difference: tuples in R but not in S
÷: division: values paired with every tuple of S
In words: a join is a product then a selection; intersection is R minus the part of R not in S. Division (÷) is also built from π, × and −.
```

Check the intersection rule on numbers:

```formula
R = {1, 2, 3} and S = {2, 3, 4}
R − S = {1}
R − (R − S) = {2, 3} = R ∩ S
where
R, S: two small example sets
{ }: a set of distinct values
−: difference
∩: intersection
In words: removing from R the part not in S leaves exactly what R and S share.
```

prompt: Using the lesson's tables, how many tuples are in the Cartesian product Student × Course (every student paired with every course)?

options.explanation: Correct. Each of the 4 students is paired with each of the 3 courses: 4 × 3 = 12.
That adds the cardinalities (4 + 3). A product pairs every tuple with every tuple, so it multiplies.
That is the size of Enrolled. A product ignores which pairs are actually enrolled.
That would be a join that keeps one match per student. A product keeps all combinations.

workedExample:
```formula
|R × S| = |R| × |S|
|Student × Course| = 4 × 3 = 12
where
R, S: any two relations
× (between relations): Cartesian product: one tuple for every pairing of a tuple of R with a tuple of S
× (between numbers): multiplication
| |: cardinality: the number of tuples in the relation inside the bars
Student: 4 tuples (Ada, Ben, Cat, Dev)
Course: 3 tuples (DB, OS, LA)
In words: every one of 4 students is paired with every one of 3 courses, giving 12 tuples.
```

The degree (number of attributes) adds instead: Student has 3 attributes and Course 3 (cid, title, dept), so the product has 6.

prompt: Student has attributes (sid, name, year) and Course has (cid, title, dept). What is the cardinality (number of tuples) of the natural join Student ⋈ Course? (⋈ with no condition is the natural join: it matches tuples on every attribute name the two relations share.)

options.explanation: A natural join with no shared attributes has no equality conditions to fail, so nothing is filtered out.
There is no join condition to pair each student with a single course.

options.text: It is undefined; natural join requires a common attribute
options.explanation: It is defined. An empty set of join attributes simply gives the product.

options.text: 12, because a natural join on no common attributes is the Cartesian product
options.explanation: Correct. The natural join is the equijoin on all shared attribute names. With none, the condition is empty (always true), so every pair survives: 4 × 3 = 12.

workedExample:
1. Natural join = equijoin on every attribute name the two headings share, keeping one copy of each.
2. Shared names between {sid, name, year} and {cid, title, dept}: **none**.
3. The join condition is the empty conjunction (an "and" of no conditions), which is true for every pair.

```formula
Student ⋈ Course = Student × Course
|Student × Course| = 4 × 3 = 12
where
⋈: natural join: match on all shared attribute names (here there are none)
× (between relations): Cartesian product: every pairing of a student with a course
× (between numbers): multiplication
| |: the number of tuples
Student, Course: the lesson's relations, with 4 and 3 tuples
In words: with nothing to match on, nothing is filtered out, so the join is the full product: 12 tuples.
```

This is also why natural join is dangerous in SQL: renaming or adding a column can silently change what it joins on.

prompt:
Which expression returns the sids of students enrolled on OS but **not** on LA? The options use this notation:

```formula
π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled))
where
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates
σ: selection: keep tuples where the condition after it is true
sid, cid: the student-id and course-code attributes
Enrolled: the enrolment relation (sid, cid)
In words: the ids of the students on OS. The options combine expressions like this with − (difference: in the left, not the right), ∩ (intersection: in both), ∧ (and) and ≠ (not equal).
```

options.explanation: The condition is tested per tuple. Every OS tuple has cid ≠ 'LA', so this returns everyone on OS, including Ada, who also takes LA.

options.text: π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled)) − π sid (σ cid='LA' (Enrolled))
options.explanation: Correct. {1, 3} − {1} = {3}. 'Not on LA' is a property of the student across tuples, which needs set difference, not a row filter.

options.text: π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled)) ∩ π sid (σ cid='LA' (Enrolled))
options.explanation: Intersection gives students on both courses: {1}, the opposite of what is asked.

options.text: π sid (σ cid='LA' (Enrolled)) − π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled))
options.explanation: Operands reversed: this gives students on LA but not OS, which is {1} − {1, 3} = ∅.

workedExample:
```formula
π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled)) = {1, 3}
π sid (σ cid='LA' (Enrolled)) = {1}
{1, 3} − {1} = {3}
where
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates
σ: selection: keep tuples where the condition is true; quoted values are literal course codes
sid, cid: the student-id and course-code attributes
Enrolled: the enrolment relation
{ }: a set of distinct values
−: difference: values on the left that are not on the right
In words: students 1 and 3 take OS, student 1 takes LA, so only student 3 (Cat) takes OS but not LA.
```

Why option A fails: σ looks at one tuple at a time. Ada's (1, OS) tuple passes the test "cid is OS and cid is not LA", so Ada wrongly appears. "Not in some other tuple" needs − (or `NOT EXISTS` in SQL).

prompt:
Which expressions are equivalent to the one below? Select all that apply.

```formula
σ year=2 (Student ⋈ Enrolled)
where
σ: selection: keep tuples where the condition after it is true
year: Student's year-of-study attribute
⋈: natural join: match tuples on shared attribute names (here sid)
Student, Enrolled: the lesson's relations
In words: the enrolments of year-2 students, with their student details. Options may also use ∪ (union) and π (projection: keep only listed attributes).
```

options.explanation: Correct. The predicate mentions only Student's attributes, so the selection can be pushed below the join.
Correct. Natural join is commutative (attributes are named, not positional), so swapping operands changes nothing.
Not even legal: ∪ needs union-compatible inputs, and Student and Enrolled have different headings.
This drops name and year before the join, so the result has only (sid, cid). Same students, different relation.

workedExample:
```formula
σ p (R ⋈ S) ≡ σ p (R) ⋈ S
R ⋈ S ≡ S ⋈ R
where
σ: selection: keep tuples where the condition is true
p: a condition that mentions only R's attributes (here year=2, on Student)
R, S: relations (here Student and Enrolled)
⋈: natural join
≡: is equivalent to: same result for any contents
In words: a filter on one input can be applied before the join, and the inputs of a join can be swapped.
```

1. Push-down rule (line 1): `year` is in Student only, so option A is valid.
2. Commutativity (line 2): option B is option A with the operands swapped.
3. Option C fails union-compatibility: ∪ (union) needs both inputs to have the same attributes.
4. Option D is a different heading: an equivalence must give exactly the same relation, attributes included. (Projecting early with π is valid only if you keep every attribute that is needed later, and here name and year are in the output.)

```formula
Enrolled ÷ π cid (Course)
where
÷: division: the student ids paired in Enrolled with every tuple of the right-hand side
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute
cid: the course-code attribute
Enrolled, Course: the lesson's relations
```

options.explanation: That is the answer for the divisor relation {DB, OS} (the CS courses). Here the divisor relation is all three courses, including LA.

workedExample:
1. Divisor relation B = all course codes, {DB, OS, LA}.
2. For each candidate sid that appears in Enrolled ({1, 2, 3}), check that its courses include all of B:

| sid | courses | all of B? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | DB, OS, LA | yes |
| 2 | DB | no |
| 3 | DB, OS | no (LA) |

3. The same with basic operators:

```formula
A = π sid (Enrolled) = {1, 2, 3}
B = π cid (Course)
B = {DB, OS, LA}
M = (A × B) − Enrolled
M = {(2,OS), (2,LA), (3,LA)}
```

prompt: A report finds "students taking every course in department X" using the double `NOT EXISTS` idiom from the lesson, driven from `student`. Department X has no courses this term. What does the query return on the lesson's data?

options.explanation: Correct. The outer `NOT EXISTS` checks for a missing X course; there are no X courses, so it is vacuously true for every row of `student`, even Dev with no enrolments.

options.text: Ada, Ben and Cat, the students with at least one enrolment
options.explanation: That is what the *algebraic* division returns, since its candidates are the students who appear in Enrolled. The SQL drives from `student` instead.

options.text: No rows, because there is nothing to take
options.explanation: Intuitive, but the logic is 'there is no X course the student lacks'. With no X courses, that is true for everyone.

options.text: An error, because the subquery is empty
options.explanation: An empty subquery is perfectly legal; `NOT EXISTS` over an empty set is simply true.

workedExample:
```sql
SELECT s.sid FROM student s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM course c
  WHERE c.dept = 'X'
    AND NOT EXISTS (...));
```

1. The outer subquery scans courses with dept X: there are none.
2. So it returns no rows, and `NOT EXISTS (empty)` is **true**.
3. That holds for every student, so all 4 sids come back.
4. Algebraic division by an empty divisor relation returns every student who appears in Enrolled:

```formula
Enrolled ÷ ∅ = π sid (Enrolled)
Enrolled ÷ ∅ = {1, 2, 3}
where
÷: division: the sids paired in Enrolled with every tuple of the divisor relation
∅: the empty set: here, the empty set of X courses
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates
sid: the student-id attribute
Enrolled: the enrolment relation
{ }: a set of distinct values
In words: "all of nothing" is true for every candidate, but the algebra's candidates are only students with an enrolment, so Dev is missing.
```
5. Lesson: decide what "all of nothing" should return, and guard with `AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM course WHERE dept = 'X')` if the answer should be empty.

prompt:
A query computes the expression below, joining on customer id. Which rewrite is valid and most useful to an optimiser?

```formula
σ c.country='UK'
  ∧ o.total > c.credit_limit
  (Customer ⋈ Order)
where
σ: selection: keep tuples where the condition is true
c.country, c.credit_limit: attributes of Customer: its country and its credit limit
o.total: an attribute of Order: the order's total
∧: and: both conditions must hold
>: is greater than
⋈: join on customer id
Customer, Order: the two relations
In words: UK customers' orders whose total exceeds the customer's credit limit.
```

options.explanation: Correct. Split the conjunction (cascade), push `country = 'UK'` down to Customer because it uses only Customer's attributes, and leave the comparison that spans both relations above the join.
The second predicate mentions `c.credit_limit`, which Order does not have, so it cannot be evaluated below the join.
Customer has no `total` attribute; only predicates over one relation's attributes can be pushed to it.

options.text: No rewrite is valid, because the predicate mentions both relations
options.explanation: The conjunction can be split (a selection on "p and q" equals a selection on p followed by one on q), and the part that mentions only Customer can then be pushed.

workedExample:
```formula
σ p∧q (X) ≡ σ q (σ p (X))
σ p (C ⋈ O) ≡ σ p (C) ⋈ O
σ q (σ p (Customer) ⋈ Order)
where
σ: selection: keep tuples where the condition is true
p: country='UK', which uses only Customer's attributes
q: total > credit_limit, which uses attributes of both relations
∧: and
X: any relation
C, O: Customer and Order
Customer, Order: the two relations
⋈: join on customer id
≡: is equivalent to: same result for any contents
In words: split the "and" (cascade), push the UK filter below the join, and keep the comparison that spans both relations above it. The last line is the rewritten query.
```

q must stay above the join (or become part of the join condition, which is the same thing as a theta join). If 10% of customers are in the UK, the join's Customer input shrinks tenfold.

prompt:
`product` has 10 rows. `discount` is NULL in 2 of them. These queries return 3 rows and 5 rows:

```sql
SELECT * FROM product
WHERE discount > 0.1;

SELECT * FROM product
WHERE NOT (discount > 0.1);
```

Why do they not add up to 10?

options.text: The two queries overlap, so some rows are counted twice
options.explanation: A row cannot satisfy both p and NOT p. There is no overlap; rows are missing, not doubled.

options.text: `NOT` is applied after `WHERE`, so it filters the wrong rows
options.explanation: `NOT` is part of the predicate, evaluated per row inside `WHERE`.

options.text: For the 2 NULL rows the predicate is *unknown*, and `WHERE` keeps only rows where it is true, so the rows where p is true plus the rows where NOT p is true no longer make up the whole relation
options.explanation: Correct. Under SQL's three-valued logic, NOT unknown is still unknown. The NULL-discount rows appear in neither result. Classical algebra assumes two-valued logic, so this identity breaks.

options.text: The optimiser used different indexes, which return different rows
options.explanation: Different plans must return the same result; an index cannot change which rows satisfy a predicate.

workedExample:
1. Non-NULL rows: 8. Of these, 3 have discount > 0.1 and 5 do not: 3 + 5 = 8.
2. NULL rows: `NULL > 0.1` is **unknown**; `NOT unknown` is **unknown**.
3. `WHERE` keeps only **true**, so the 2 NULL rows appear in neither query.
4. To cover everything: `WHERE NOT (discount > 0.1) OR discount IS NULL`, or `COALESCE(discount, 0) <= 0.1`.
